passages.speaker: Nahusha (narrating Yayati)
events: Yayati grows old and asks his sons for their youth
Yayati returns youth to his son and returns the throne
passages.summary: Yayati, king and lover of pleasure, is struck old before his time. He begs his sons to lend him their youth; only Purukutsa agrees. Yayati rules for a thousand more years, discovers that desire is not exhausted by being fed, and returns the youth to his son, renouncing the throne. The parable closes with the observation that desire is insatiable.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, the story of Yayati

passages.section: Sambhava Parva — the birth of Karna
passages.speaker: narrator
events: Kunti abandons the infant
Kunti's later promise that the child would be protected by his armour
passages.summary: Kunti, unmarried and frightened, places her infant by the river rather than face the consequences of her situation. The child is found and raised by a charioteer's family. The abandonment shapes every later choice Karna makes: his hunger for recognition, his insistence on loyalty to the man who honoured him when the world did not.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, the birth and abandonment of Karna

passages.speaker: Draupadi / narrating voice
events: Karna attempts the bow and is refused
Arjuna as a brahmin wins the contest
Draupadi rejects Karna
passages.summary: At Draupadi's marriage contest, Karna steps forward and is told he is not eligible because of his accepted birth. Draupadi refuses him publicly. The moment is one of the text's clearest illustrations of how a single rule of belonging can produce a grievance that outlives everyone present.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, Draupadi's svayamvara
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Drona / Arjuna
events: Ekalavya practices alone before a clay image
Ekalavya cuts off his own thumb as guru-dakshina
passages.summary: A young Nishada learns archery by watching and practising before a clay image of his teacher. Drona, pressed by Arjuna's claim to be the best, collects a fee: the boy's right thumb. Ekalavya cuts it off without a word. The episode is the text's hardest question about what a teacher owes, and about the lengths to which competence is policed.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, Ekalavya and the guru-dakshina

passages.speaker: Devavrata (Bhishma)
events: Devavrata renounces the throne
He swears the vow of lifelong celibacy so that there is no dispute over succession
passages.summary: To clear his father's path to a marriage he wants, the crown prince renounces the throne and then, because renunciation alone is not enough, swears a vow that removes any future claim through him. The vow solves the immediate problem and creates the conditions for the war two generations later. It is the text's most concentrated study of a promise that outlives its reason.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, Bhishma's vow

passages.speaker: Amba
events: Amba is taken at a svayamvara and returned
Amba vows to be the cause of Bhishma's death
She is reborn as Shikhandi
passages.summary: Abandoned by the king she chose, Amba demands that Bhishma take responsibility for ruining her life; he refuses, holding that he acted within his duty. She pursues the grievance across a lifetime and into another body. Bhishma's later refusal to fight Shikhandi is the direct consequence of a wrong he never acknowledged as his.
passages.source_reference: Adi Parva — Sambhava Parva, the story of Amba and Shikhandi

passages.section: Vidura's warning before the dice game
passages.speaker: Vidura
events: Vidura warns the king against the invitation
Dhritarashtra overrules him and permits the game
passages.summary: Vidura tells his brother plainly that the invitation to a dice game is a trap and that a king who permits it will answer for what follows. Dhritarashtra, wanting both the outcome and an excuse, allows the game and then asks to be reassured that all will be well. The scene is the text's model of counsel given, heard, and not acted on.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — Vidura's counsel to Dhritarashtra before the dice game
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Yudhishthira / Shakuni
events: Yudhishthira wagers and loses his kingdom
He wagers his brothers
He wagers himself and then Draupadi
passages.summary: Knowing the dice are loaded, Yudhishthira continues to throw, moving from wealth to brothers to himself and finally to Draupadi. Each round he is offered a way out and does not take it. The text does not treat this as a single mistake: it is a sequence of choices, and the narration keeps asking why a man known for truth kept playing.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — the great dice game
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Draupadi
events: Draupadi asks whether Yudhishthira lost himself before he could stake her
The assembly does not answer
passages.summary: Dragged into the hall, Draupadi puts a narrow legal question: could her husband stake her, if he had already staked and lost himself? The learned men of the court are silent — not because they cannot answer, but because answering would cost them. Her question turns a procedural dispute into a test of everyone present.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — Draupadi's question after the dice game
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Dushasana / Karna
events: Dushasana drags Draupadi into the hall
Karna declares her status
Bhima swears an oath
passages.summary: In the middle of the court, Draupadi asks for protection and receives commentary instead. Karna, who has his own grievance, tells her that her condition is the result of her husband's gambling. Bhima answers with an oath. The scene is the hinge of the whole epic: every later decision about the war is traceable to what the court did and did not do here.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — the humiliation of Draupadi

passages.speaker: Shishupala's objector / narrating voice
events: Shishupala objects to Krishna's honour
Krishna kills Shishupala
Bhishma defends the choice
passages.summary: Shishupala insults Krishna a hundred times and is killed on the hundred-and-first, fulfilling a vow Krishna had sworn to Shishupala's mother. The episode is often read as forgiveness with a limit; it is also a warning about how long a promise of tolerance can be held hostage by the person testing it.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — the rajasuya and the death of Shishupala

passages.speaker: Krishna / narrating voice
events: Krishna identifies the only way to kill Jarasandha
Bhima tears him apart in wrestling
passages.summary: Before the rajasuya can be completed, one stubborn king must be removed. Krishna works out the single weakness and hands the analysis to Bhima, who executes it. The passage separates planning from execution and shows counsel being converted into action by someone with the capacity to act.
passages.source_reference: Sabha Parva — the killing of Jarasandha
